newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Canada, Australia to outflank U.S..
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Canada, Australia to outflank U.S..

text.p: Australian and Canadian government bonds, revelling in steady U.S. interest rates, have further to gain against Treasuries, analysts said on Friday.

But with the recent rally in both markets looking strained, investors will have to move fast, particularly if U.S. economic growth decelerates in the second half of 1996 as the Federal Reserve predicts, they said.
"The Australian market may have a little bit further to go, partly because there's more yield enhancement there," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ in London.
"There also seems to be a fair degree of stability in the currency despite it having failed to push through the US$0.80 mark," he said.
Australian and Canadian bonds have outstripped their dollar bloc cousin all summer as the central banks in each country sliced interest rates while the Fed held fast.

The spread between the yields on 10-year Australian and U.S. bonds has shrunk to around 117 basis points from 260 at the beginning of April. The Canada/U.S. gap has crunched to around 50 basis point from about 120 in the same time.

Hannah said while wage pressures may begin to surface in Australia, the underlying inflation picture remains benign. Third quarter inflation data due at the end of October could provide the trigger for a 50 basis point cut from the 7.00 percent cash rate, he said.

"I think the spread may well test the 100 basis point level...in the next one to three months," Hannah said. "It's possible it could go below that if there are signs of exchange rate stability," he said.
The Australian dollar has failed to break decisively through US$0.80 cents in three attempts in May, June and early September but it has not recoiled. It was quoted at US$0.79 at 1122 GMT.
Hannah was not as positive for Canadian bonds, simply because they have hurtled ahead so far so fast.
"I would very much doubt whether it would trade much below 50 basis points despite the absence of a Fed move and continued speculation about a further cut in Canada," he said.
Michael Burke, bond strategist at Citibank in London, took the opposite view, favouring Canadian over Australian bonds.

He said the Canadian central bank could cut interest rates further, flaunting its renewed independence with monetary policy against a steadfast U.S. The call rate currently stands at 3.75-4.25 percent.

Buffering a bright spread outlook was Canada's sparkling export performance which will allow it to continue in its rigorous deficit cutting programme, Burke said. Canada shipped a record C$22.51 billion worth of goods to the world in July, helped by a surge in lumber and auto part exports to the United States.
"Market investors are very bullish partly for reasons of external accounts and I think that's justified," said Burke.
He said the Canada/U.S. spread could get as narrow as 35 basis points in the short term but if the U.S. economy begins to slow, Canadian exports will slow as well.
It is this scenario that Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking, favours. He said beyond the next month, Treasuries will begin to win back ground.
"I think we are going to see some deceleration of growth coming through in the second half data," he said. Australian and Canadian data was likely to show a pickup.

"These markets which have been at the extreme favourable end of their trading ranges relative to U.S. Treasuries, are probably going to revert to a more normal relationship," he said. Lewis expects the Canada/T-note spread to spring to 75 basis points by the end of October and the Australin/T-note spread to 140 by the end of the year.
